tells: Each paragraph picks up the last ('uses the same word', 'With powers set aside'), names the speaker before each quotation and says what it means, and leaves out the comma before 'and' ('worship to be something other than God Himself" and he recalls'), all as in the reference.

Opens by picking up a list ('The first is sight'), restates the prayer in plain words, has the Sheikh raise the objection himself and then answers it calmly in plain exposition, as the reference does with the cattle verse.
'But our knowledge of tawhid' — Author A does not open sentences with 'But'; would write 'Our knowledge of tawhid ... is still not'
'And Surah Yunus gives them a second name' — opening a sentence with 'And' is spoken phrasing Author A avoids; would write 'Surah Yunus adds to their names'

'Surah Fatir adds: "Only those of Allah's servants having knowledge fear Him"' — puts a claim, a colon and a quotation in one sentence; Author A writes a lead-in sentence and sets the verse on its own ('The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.')
'very hard to grasp' — an intensifier Author A leaves out; would write 'hard to grasp'

Raises the reader's concern and answers it straight away ('Surah al-Nisaʾ answers that concern'), introduces the verse and then glosses it rank by rank with the Sheikh's reading, and ties it back to an earlier verse, the way the reference connects its points.

'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide. Neither makes powers the aim of the path.' — a neat antithesis plus a summary line to close the paragraph; Author A stops on the last point of substance

'Mutahhari's words show why seeking them would be: the goal has become something other than God' — a clumsy sentence that hangs on a colon; Author A writes a complete clause ('Mutahhari explains why seeking them would be so')
'For him the feats are beside the point: something a student should look past when deciding whom to trust' — stacks a claim, a colon and an appositive gloss; Author A writes two plain sentences

'Sheikh Bahmanpour calls such powers shirk and Mutahhari's words show why ... ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi, discussing ...' — packs three authorities into one paragraph with no step between them; Author A gives each source its own paragraph

Short declarative sentences, no comma before 'and', a quotation introduced and then glossed ('Shirk, setting up a partner beside God, is the gravest charge in Islam'), and the paragraph ends on that gloss with no editorial comment.
'The reward.' — a verbless fragment used as a signpost; Author A writes full sentences ('Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.')
'in the lecturer's reading' — Author A always names him ('Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as...')

'The second gift is a different kind of life.' / 'The third gift is peace.' — each paragraph ends on a teaser for the next item, building mild suspense; Author A gives each item its own paragraph, opening on it ('The first is...', 'The second is...')
'rise above the concerns that infect everyone else' — heated wording, sharper and more judging of others than Author A's level register

A lead-in sentence before each quoted verse ('Surah Fatir describes the same people by what they feel.', 'Imam ʿAli (as) describes what these friends see'), as in 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.' No 'But' or 'And' openings and no intensifiers.

Says the Sheikh 'reads' the text, introduces the quotation and then glosses it, names the Arabic term followed by its English with no comma before 'and' ('inqitaʿ, being cut off and the Munajat'), and settles the misreading in a plain closing sentence, all as in the reference.

Points back across the book's structure ('Part One began with... Chapter Two showed') as the introduction does, keeps lists without an Oxford comma, and reuses the reference's own phrase 'already on our lips'. The recap ending is borderline.

'Requests this high raise a difficulty and Sheikh Bahmanpour states it himself' has the reference's comma-less 'and' and its habit of letting the Sheikh raise the objection. Quotations are introduced by name and followed by a plain gloss ('Need is the only reason the prayer gives for coming').
